Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that, despite Apple's claims of reviewing app metadata, "obvious" rating manipulation on the App Store has gone undetected.

He notes that, although he wasn't actively hunting for scams on the App Store, he has come across them with surprising frequency, and shares a recent example as proof…

The App Store as a 'safe and trusted place'

Apple has consistently resisted any antitrust measures that would involve third-party iPhone app stores or sideloading, only relenting when legally compelled to do so. Even so, the company continues to maintain its position.

The company claims its motivation isn't money, but rather a desire to protect iPhone users from malware. For instance, the company claimed last year to have blocked more than $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, multiple developers have questioned the notion that the App Store is a safe place, pointing to numerous scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, three customers sued Apple after a fake wallet app drained their Bitcoin.

App Store rating manipulation

App Store rating manipulation is a long-standing problem, with some companies in China renting iPhone farms to download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Jeff Johnson, known for his StopTheMadness Safari extension, points to what he calls the latest example of "widespread and obvious" rating manipulation on the App Store. He cites the TabControl Extension as a recent case.

He says that when he stumbled upon the app, it was already the 12th highest paid Safari extension on the US Mac App Store, and was using what appear to be AI-generated fake screenshots.

Another thing you should notice is the '4.9 out of 5 stars' rating in the fake screenshots, which makes people think it's the app's user rating on the App Store… Using fake App Store screenshots to make false claims is a common scam tactic I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple not only reviews the app itself, but also reviews its App Store listing data and metadata, including screenshots, and the claims in these scam app screenshots are obviously absurd, yet Apple still approved them… Apple claims its App Store protects users from dishonest developers. If the App Store review fails to do this, then what is it actually doing? In reality, the App Store review doesn't need to be as in-depth as what I've done. The '4.9 out of 5 stars' in the screenshot should be a red flag. Apple has records of all ratings and reviews for all countries, so they know this is false advertising. I don't even need to download the app to know the developer intends to scam people.

As he points out, if a developer is trying to scam you from the very start with their app marketing, you certainly wouldn't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, detecting every instance of App Store fraud will never be possible, but fake reviews are extremely common, and examples like this one should be glaringly obvious to Apple, making it hard to understand how the extension passed review in the first place.

Apple needs to at least establish a mechanism whereby any app that breaks into the top charts automatically triggers a fresh, more rigorous review, examining both the app itself and the claims it makes.
